findings.text: The first paragraph tells a newcomer what Athena is and what sets it apart. This is the only description of Athena on the page: there is no example of a request and the change it produced, and no cost figures.
findings.source: "Athena is an open-source system, written in Rust, that turns a short request into a change to a code repository. It shows how it read the request, has one AI model do the work and a different one check it, and records what each step cost."

findings.text: Someone arriving at Athena's address gets a page whose title and nearly all of whose content are about a different project. Three paragraphs explain the link, but almost everything after them is firstmate internals, so a reader can easily lose track of which tool the page is selling.
findings.source: <title>Athena explains how firstmate handles work</title> and the header line "This page is that study of firstmate."

findings.text: This gives the 'why it matters': the page itself is evidence that Athena's output can be checked. The bracketed claim ids and source links to pinned lines back it up, but the page never says why a newcomer would want such a study of their own project.
findings.source: "Athena made this study of firstmate to show that it can read an unfamiliar project and explain it with every statement traced to a claim, and every claim to lines in the project's own files."

findings.text: The next steps are concrete and linked from the top of the page. But they skip how to get the checkout, what setup needs (for example a Rust toolchain or model access), and what `athena ask` will do to the repository it runs in.
findings.source: Next steps: "Install Athena from a checkout of its repository: ./setup.sh" and "Try it with a one-line request: athena ask \"add a changelog\""

findings.text: Terms are defined before they are used, which helps. But firstmate's own vocabulary (captain, yolo, green/red, secondmate) and these hedging notes make the 'Start here' section heavy going for anyone who doesn't already use firstmate.
findings.source: Heading "Words used first" and the dd for "in scope": "The cited instruction does not say what makes work in scope, so this page gives no test for it."

findings.text: The state cards, transition cards and counter sections are detailed down to exit codes. That suits someone checking firstmate's design, but it is far more than a newcomer needs to decide whether to try Athena.
findings.source: Transitions card t2: "the spawn is deferred with exit 75 and the item stays queued. A spawn that cannot take the project lock, or cannot read the capacity declaration, exits 1 instead and does not wait."

findings.text: The page openly says the study read firstmate's files without running anything. That makes it more trustworthy, though the 'not run' tags and finding ids (f1–f3) are Athena's internal terms and aren't explained.
findings.source: Heading "Limits of this study": "This study read the pinned tree only... no failure or retry edge was observed; every claim is marked read."

findings.text: This closing section points to a `studies/` folder without saying which repository holds it, so it is useless to a newcomer.
findings.source: Heading "About this page": "is the name of the folder under studies/ that holds the data this page is generated from."
